title: Random or multiple cylinder misfire
detail: The engine computer detected misfires on more than one cylinder (or could not tell which one). A misfire means fuel in a cylinder did not burn properly.
implications: You may feel shaking, rough idle, power loss, or a flashing engine light. Driving with heavy misfires can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter.
actions: Check spark plugs and ignition coils first; they are the most common cause
If the engine light flashes, reduce load and get it checked promptly
Ask a mechanic to check fuel delivery and compression if plugs and coils are fine

title: System too lean, bank 1
detail: The engine is getting too much air (or too little fuel) on bank 1, so the computer is adding extra fuel to compensate.
implications: Possible rough idle, hesitation, or poor fuel economy. Long-term lean running can overheat engine parts.
actions: Listen and look for vacuum or intake air leaks (hoses, gaskets)
Check the mass airflow sensor; cleaning it sometimes helps
Ask a mechanic to check fuel pressure and oxygen sensors

title: System too lean, bank 2
detail: Same lean condition as P0171 but on bank 2 (the other side of a V engine). Both banks lean at once usually points to a shared cause.
implications: Rough idle, hesitation, poor fuel economy. Both banks affected means check shared parts first.
actions: Check for intake air leaks affecting the whole engine
Check the mass airflow sensor and fuel pressure
Ask a mechanic to read live fuel-trim data at idle and cruise

title: System too rich, bank 1
detail: The engine is getting too much fuel (or too little air) on bank 1, so the computer is cutting fuel back.
implications: Possible black exhaust smoke, fuel smell, fouled spark plugs, or failed emissions test.
actions: Check the air filter and intake for blockages
A leaking fuel injector is a common cause; ask a mechanic to test them
Have oxygen sensors checked if the problem persists

title: System too rich, bank 2
detail: Same rich condition as P0172 but on bank 2. Both banks rich at once usually points to a shared cause.
implications: Fuel smell, black smoke, fouled plugs, poor fuel economy.
actions: Check the air filter and fuel pressure regulator
Ask a mechanic to test injectors and oxygen sensors

title: Catalyst efficiency below threshold, bank 1
detail: The catalytic converter on bank 1 is no longer cleaning exhaust gases well enough. The computer compares the two oxygen sensors to judge this.
implications: Often no driving symptoms at first, but the car will fail an emissions inspection. A bad converter can be a symptom of an engine problem upstream.
actions: Rule out exhaust leaks and faulty oxygen sensors before replacing the converter
Fix any misfire or rich-running codes first; they kill converters
Converter replacement is a mechanic job; get an emissions diagnosis

title: Catalyst efficiency below threshold, bank 2
detail: Same converter-efficiency problem as P0420 but on bank 2.
implications: Emissions failure risk; usually no immediate driving symptoms.
actions: Check oxygen sensors and exhaust leaks on bank 2 first
Fix upstream misfire or fuel codes before condemning the converter

title: Exhaust gas recirculation flow insufficient
detail: The EGR system, which feeds a little exhaust back into the engine to cut emissions, is not flowing enough gas.
implications: Possible rough idle, pinging under load, or higher emissions. Often just carbon buildup.
actions: EGR passages and valves clog with carbon; cleaning may fix it
Check EGR vacuum hoses and electrical connector
Ask a mechanic to test EGR valve operation

title: Evaporative emission system malfunction
detail: The system that traps fuel vapors from the tank has a general fault. Vapors should be stored and burned, not vented.
implications: Usually no driving symptoms; fuel smell is possible. Emissions-related.
actions: Check that the fuel cap is tight and its seal is not cracked
Look for cracked or disconnected vapor hoses near the tank
Ask a mechanic for a smoke test to find the leak

title: Evaporative emission system small leak
detail: A small leak was found in the fuel-vapor system, often as simple as a loose fuel cap.
implications: Rarely affects driving; mainly an emissions fault.
actions: Tighten or replace the fuel cap, then drive a few days and re-scan
Inspect vapor hoses for cracks if the code returns
A smoke test finds leaks a visual check misses

title: Evaporative vent control circuit issue
detail: The vent valve that lets the vapor system breathe is not responding as expected (stuck, blocked, or electrical fault).
implications: Usually no symptoms; refueling may be slow if the vent is stuck shut.
actions: Check the vent valve connector and wiring
Spider webs and dirt can block the vent filter; inspect it
Ask a mechanic to command the valve and test it

title: Evaporative emission system large leak
detail: A large leak in the fuel-vapor system: missing fuel cap, broken hose, or stuck-open purge valve.
implications: Possible fuel smell; otherwise usually no driving symptoms.
actions: Check the fuel cap first: present, tight, seal intact
Look for disconnected or split hoses around the tank and engine
Ask a mechanic for a smoke test if nothing is visible

title: Evaporative emission system very small leak
detail: A tiny leak in the fuel-vapor system, at the detection limit. Often a aging fuel-cap seal.
implications: No driving symptoms; purely an emissions matter.
actions: Replace the fuel cap if it is old; clear and re-scan after a few drives
A smoke test is the reliable way to find pinhole leaks

title: Intake air temperature sensor high input
detail: The intake-air temperature reading is impossibly high, which means the sensor circuit is likely open or unplugged.
implications: The computer miscalculates air density, so fueling and performance suffer.
actions: Find the sensor on the intake and check its connector
Check wiring for breaks or corrosion
The sensor itself is cheap; replace if the circuit is fine

title: Engine coolant temperature sensor high input
detail: The coolant-temperature reading is impossibly high, which means the sensor circuit is likely open or unplugged.
implications: Wrong temperature data can cause hard starting, poor fueling, and the dashboard gauge reading wrong.
actions: Check the coolant sensor connector and wiring
Do not confuse with real overheating: check the gauge and coolant level
Replace the sensor if the circuit tests fine

title: Coolant thermostat below regulating temperature
detail: The engine takes too long to warm up, usually because the thermostat is stuck open and coolant circulates too freely.
implications: Higher fuel consumption, weak cabin heat, extra engine wear, possible emissions failure.
actions: A stuck-open thermostat is the classic cause; replacement is routine
Check coolant level first; low coolant mimics this
Do not ignore: a cold-running engine wears faster

title: Oxygen sensor low voltage, bank 1 sensor 1
detail: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 is stuck reading lean (low voltage). The sensor, its heater, or its wiring may have failed.
implications: Poor fuel control, hesitation, worse economy, possible catalyst damage over time.
actions: Check the sensor connector and wiring for damage
Exhaust leaks near the sensor fake a lean reading; rule those out
Replace the sensor if wiring and exhaust are fine

title: Oxygen sensor high voltage, bank 1 sensor 1
detail: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 is stuck reading rich (high voltage).
implications: The computer may over-lean the mixture; drivability and economy suffer.
actions: Check for wiring shorts and connector contamination (coolant, oil)
Rule out genuinely rich running (see P0172 causes) first
Replace the sensor if the engine is actually running normally

title: Oxygen sensor heater circuit, bank 1 sensor 2
detail: The heater that brings the downstream oxygen sensor up to temperature quickly has an electrical fault.
implications: Slow sensor warm-up; usually no driving symptoms. Emissions-related.
actions: Check the heater fuse and the sensor connector
Measure heater resistance if you have a meter, or ask a mechanic
Sensor replacement fixes most cases

title: Injector circuit malfunction, cylinder 1
detail: The electrical circuit driving fuel injector 1 is open, shorted, or the injector coil failed.
implications: That cylinder gets no (or uncontrolled) fuel: rough running, power loss, misfire codes alongside.
actions: Check the injector connector and wiring on cylinder 1
An injector resistance test confirms a dead coil
Wiring repairs and injector replacement are mechanic jobs

title: Ignition coil primary circuit, cylinder 1
detail: The coil that fires cylinder 1 has a primary-circuit electrical fault.
implications: Misfire on that cylinder: shaking, flashing engine light, catalyst risk.
actions: Swap the coil with another cylinder and see if the misfire moves
Check the coil connector and wiring
Replace the faulty coil; consider plugs at the same time

title: Idle speed lower than expected
detail: The engine idles slower than the computer wants. Air is not getting past the throttle as expected.
implications: Rough or stalling idle, vibration at stoplights.
actions: Clean carbon from the throttle body and idle passages
Check for vacuum leaks and sticky idle valves
An idle relearn procedure may be needed after cleaning

title: Idle speed higher than expected
detail: The engine idles faster than the computer wants. Extra air is entering somewhere.
implications: High idle, harsh gear engagement in automatics.
actions: Check for vacuum leaks and a sticking throttle plate
Clean the throttle body and check the idle valve
An idle relearn procedure may be needed after repair

title: System voltage low
detail: Electrical system voltage dropped too low: weak battery, failing alternator, or bad connections.
implications: Dim lights, slow cranking, random electronic glitches, possible stalling.
actions: Check battery terminals for corrosion and tightness
Measure voltage: about 12.6 V off, 13.7-14.7 V running
Have the battery and alternator tested; replace as needed

title: Transmission control system requested MIL
detail: The transmission computer found a fault and asked the engine computer to switch the engine light on. The real detail lives in the transmission module.
implications: Possible harsh or limited shifting; the transmission may enter limp mode.
actions: Read transmission-specific codes with a capable scanner
Check transmission fluid level and condition
Transmission diagnosis is a specialist job; avoid hard driving

title: Lost communication with engine computer
detail: A module on the car network stopped talking to the engine computer. Often wiring, power, ground, or a failed module.
implications: Warning lights, disabled assists, no-start in bad cases. Intermittent at first.
actions: Check battery voltage and main grounds; low voltage scrambles networks
Look for damaged CAN wiring, especially after repairs or accidents
Network faults need wiring diagrams; involve a specialist early
